title: 22. Interview: Twitter/X — Social Media Feed System (deep dive)
summary: Interview Q&A for Twitter/X — Social Media Feed System (deep dive) — 15 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 15 Twitter/X — Social Media Feed System (deep dive) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: 15 Interview Questions with Answers
sections.body:
### Q1: How would you design the Twitter home timeline?

**Answer:** Hybrid fan-out approach. Regular users (<10K followers): fan-out on write — when they tweet, push to all followers' Redis timeline caches. Celebrities: fan-out on read — when user opens timeline, fetch celebrity tweets on-the-fly. Home timeline = merge(cached_timeline + celebrity_tweets), sorted by ranking score. Cache stores tweet IDs (not full tweets) to save memory.

### Q2: How does Twitter handle 500M tweets/day?

**Answer:** (1) **Sharding** — tweets sharded by user_id or tweet_id across Cassandra clusters. (2) **Write path** — tweet → Kafka → async fan-out. (3) **Caching** — Redis clusters for hot data. (4) **CDN** — media served via CDN. (5) **Rate limiting** — prevent abuse. Architecture: Tweet Service → Kafka → Fan-out Workers → Redis. Writes are async; reads are from cache.

### Q3: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read?

**Answer:** **Write**: Pre-compute timelines when tweet is created. Fast reads, slow writes for popular users. O(followers) writes per tweet. **Read**: Compute timeline at read time by querying all followed users. Slow reads, fast writes. O(following) queries per read. **Hybrid (Twitter)**: Write for regular users, read for celebrities. Optimal balance for the 99% case.

### Q4: How would you handle celebrity tweets?

**Answer:** Don't fan-out for celebrities (millions of followers). When user requests timeline: (1) Get pre-computed cache, (2) Identify celebrity follows, (3) Fetch their recent tweets (small query per celebrity), (4) Merge. Why: Fan-out for 50M followers would take too long and waste resources. Trade-off: slightly slower read for users following celebrities.

### Q5: How would you design Twitter Search?

**Answer:** (1) **Inverted index** (Elasticsearch) — index tweets by words/hashtags. (2) **Real-time indexing** — new tweets indexed within seconds. (3) **Ranking** — recency + engagement + relevance. (4) **Typeahead** — autocomplete with Trie. (5) **Sharding** — index sharded by time (recent data on dedicated shards). Early bird index: precomputed results for trending searches.

### Q6: How do you compute trending topics?

**Answer:** Sliding window count of hashtags/topics. Count occurrences in last N minutes. Score = (current_rate - baseline_rate) / baseline. This catches spikes, not just popular topics. Implementation: Kafka → Spark Streaming → count per window → rank by velocity. Personalization: trending per country/interest. Filter: remove spam, duplicates.

### Q7: How would you design the notification system?

**Answer:** (1) **Event-driven** — user actions → Kafka events → notification workers. (2) **Aggregation** — batch similar notifications ("A and 5 others liked"). (3) **Priority** — DMs > mentions > replies > likes. (4) **Delivery** — push notifications (APNS/FCM), in-app, email digest. (5) **Preferences** — users control which notifications. Storage: Cassandra (recent) + cold storage.

### Q8: How do you ensure consistency in likes/retweet counts?

**Answer:** Eventual consistency with Redis counters. When user likes: (1) Redis INCR for quick count. (2) Async write to persistent store. (3) Deduplication set (user can't like twice). For hot tweets with millions of likes: approximate counting using HyperLogLog or counter sharding. Accept small inconsistency for performance.

### Q9: How would you handle media storage?

**Answer:** Upload: Client → presigned S3 URL → direct upload to S3. Processing: S3 event → Lambda/worker → resize (4 sizes), transcode video (HLS). Storage: S3 + CDN (CloudFront). Metadata: tweet → media_id mapping in DB. Video: HLS adaptive bitrate, CDN edge caching. Cost optimization: S3 lifecycle policies (infrequent access after 30 days).

### Q10: How would you design direct messaging?

**Answer:** Real-time: WebSocket connections. Storage: conversation_id → messages (ordered by timestamp). sharded by conversation_id. Encryption: end-to-end encryption (Signal protocol). Group DMs: fan-out messages to all participants. Read receipts: separate tracking table. Notification: push when offline. History: pagination with cursor (message_id-based).

### Q11: How do you handle tweet deletion?

**Answer:** Soft delete: mark as deleted in DB, lazy remove from timelines. Remove from search index immediately. Cached timelines: skip deleted tweets at read time (cheaper than traversing all follower caches). Media: async cleanup from S3/CDN. Retweets of deleted tweets: show "Tweet unavailable." GDPR: permanent deletion with audit trail.

### Q12: Database schema for Twitter?

**Answer:** **Users table**: user_id (PK), username, bio, followers_count, following_count. **Tweets table**: tweet_id (PK), user_id, content, created_at, reply_to_id, media_ids. **Follows table**: follower_id + following_id (composite PK). **Likes table**: user_id + tweet_id. **Timeline cache**: Redis sorted set per user (score=timestamp, value=tweet_id). Tweets in Cassandra (high write throughput), users in PostgreSQL.

### Q13: How do you scale the follow graph?

**Answer:** Graph stored in Cassandra/Redis. Table: follows(follower_id, following_id, timestamp). Queries: (1) Who does user follow? → partition by follower_id. (2) Who follows user? → partition by following_id. Need both tables for both directions. For users with millions of followers: paginated queries. Graph analytics (friend-of-friend): run offline in Spark, cache recommendations.

### Q14: How would you implement rate limiting?

**Answer:** Multi-level: (1) **API gateway** — global limits per IP. (2) **User-level** — per-endpoint limits (300 tweets/hour, 1500 reads/15min). (3) **Application-level** — per app/API key. Algorithm: Token bucket or sliding window counter. Storage: Redis (INCR with TTL). Response: HTTP 429 with Retry-After header and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers.

### Q15: How do you handle a Super Bowl-type traffic spike?

**Answer:** (1) **Auto-scaling** — Kubernetes HPA for API servers. (2) **Rate limiting** — degrade gracefully. (3) **Feature degradation** — disable search ranking, show simpler timeline. (4) **Cached responses** — serve stale data for trending topics. (5) **Queue backpressure** — Kafka absorbs write spikes. (6) **CDN** — cache GET responses at edge. (7) **Pre-warming** — scale up before known events. (8) **Circuit breakers** — protect downstream services.

**Next Chapter: [Design Netflix →](02_Netflix.md)**
